I specialize in Mathematical Physics!

Dr. Kaushlendra Kumar

DFG Walter-Benjamin Research Fellow — School of Mathematical Sciences, QMUL London

I am a mathematical physicist working at the intersection of geometry, gauge theory, and fundamental physics. My research spans classical and quantum aspects of Yang–Mills theory, the geometry of noncommutative and quantum spaces, and emergent gravity in matrix models. A recurring theme across these areas is the use of sophisticated mathematical structures—Lie groups, spectral triples, division algebras—to extract new physical insight. My current project with Shahn Majid explores particle physics through the lens of Quantum Riemannian Geometry. I hold a PhD (Magna cum Laude) from Leibniz University Hannover and have held positions at Humboldt University Berlin and the Erwin Schrödinger Institute, Vienna.

What is Mathematical Physics?

This is an ongoing enterprise whose goal is to understand and encode the observed physical phenomena into a “set of fundamental principles” using the language of mathematics. Having thus established some of the elements of such a “set” using known experimental results, it then tries to predict future outcomes using those elements. This has been an astoundingly successful endeavour over the last few centuries! We have been able to understand the workings of natural laws across a wide spectrum of phenomena—from the unimaginably tiny subatomic world to the humongous and ever-increasing expanse of the cosmos—in terms of mathematical equations. The first revolution in, if not the beginning of, this enterprise can be attributed to Sir Isaac Newton, who devised calculus to explain the everyday motion of objects including classical gravity. Since then there have been several giants like Leonhard Euler, James Clerk Maxwell, Max Planck, Albert Einstein, Erwin Schrödinger, Paul Dirac, Richard Feynman, Stephen Hawking and many others who have carried the enterprise on their shoulders. At present, we have two sets of fundamental physics theories that have been immensely successful: the Standard Model of particle physics, and Einstein’s General Relativity, which accurately describes gravity as the curvature of spacetime. The hunt for a unified theory encompassing both has been the holy grail for mathematical physicists for decades. Prominent candidates include String Theory, Loop Quantum Gravity, and Noncommutative Geometry, but none have yet been fully successful—the hunt is still on.
